content: Chromium(III) oxide, with the chemical formula Cr₂O₃, is an inorganic compound and one of the primary oxides of chromium. It serves as a widely utilized precursor for the synthesis of other chromium-based compounds. In its natural form, it is found as a rare mineral called eskolaite. Additionally, there are very rare chromium oxyhydroxide minerals, such as bracewellite, guyanaite, and grimaldiite, which are also known to exist. Cr₂O₃ adopts the corundum crystal structure, characterized by cubic close-packed oxide ions with two-thirds of the octahedral voids occupied by chromium ions. This compound exhibits antiferromagnetic properties up to a temperature of 307 K, known as the Néel temperature. Chromium(III) oxide is an amphoteric oxide, meaning it can react with both acids and bases. When dissolved in acids, it forms chromium(III) salts, while in molten alkali, it produces chromites. The compound was first synthesized in 1838 by the Parisian chemists Pannetier and Binet through a secretive process. Industrially, it is produced from the mineral chromite, (Fe,Mg)Cr₂O₄, which is mined in regions such as southern Africa, Asia, Turkey, and Cuba. The production process involves the oxidation of chromite in air to form sodium dichromate (Na₂Cr₂O₇), which is subsequently reduced using carbon or sulfur. Chromium oxide can also be reduced to elemental chromium metal via the thermite reaction. However, this process is less commonly employed compared to the use of iron oxides like Fe₂O₃ and Fe₃O₄. Unlike iron oxide thermites, chromium oxide thermites produce minimal sparks, smoke, or sound, but emit an intense, blinding light. Due to the extremely high melting point of chromium, casting chromium via the thermite process is impractical. When used as a pigment, chromium(III) oxide is commonly referred to as chrome green or institutional green. Historically, it was known as viridian when it was first discovered.
